# Chapter 1 Gold 

## 1.  Summary 

The year 2011 marked a decade since the gold market balance shifted into fundamental surplus.  The size of the surplus, however, did not expand last year as it did in 2010 and most notably in 2009, but actually dropped by 21% to 1,138 tonnes. 

One key factor behind this radical end to expansion was an actual loss of one of the important sources of gold supply – official sector sales, which primarily represent the actions of central banks in various countries.  The official sector was a net seller for six consecutive years between 2002 and 2007 before turning into a net buyer in 2008 and 2009.  In 2010, it changed again, but the scale of sales was insignificant.  And, after this short break, central banks returned with even greater appetite for gold in 2011.  Their net purchases of slightly over 400 tonnes had a significant negative impact on the overall level of global gold supply last year.  Prior to 2011, sales of gold by central banks averaged approximately 300 t/y.  In some years, the sector even contributed of up to 20% of global gold supply. 

With this source of supply gone, global gold supply reduced in volume as none of the other three major sources were able to fill the void.  Specifically, gold miners, which had been ramping up output for three years, managed to increase their contribution by only 38 tonnes year-on-year or 1.5%.  An additional 12 tonnes were brought to the market due to the first net expansion of the global gold producer hedge book in more than ten years, this contrasting with a 121 tonnes contraction of producers’ hedges in 2010.  And the additional 171 tonnes that these two sources supplied to the gold market in 2011 was partly offset by a fall in secondary output where year-on-year volumes declined by 58 tonnes.  Adding in the negative sales from the official sector, world gold supply fell by 7.5% last year to a total of 3,892 tonnes. 

It was only because fabrication demand was also weak in 2011 that the market surplus did not shrink by even more.  Fairly speaking, the overall impact that this part of the supply-demand equation had on the change in the size of market balance was muted; total fabrication demand fell by 0.5% last year to 2,754 tonnes.  Lacklustre demand for jewellery was the largest absolute driver of this decline.  The total drop would have been more substantial had jewellery’s fall not been offset by brisk growth in demand for gold coins which jumped by 13% year-on-year.  This area of offtake fully recouped the losses incurred in the 2010, with annual demand hitting a new record of 240 tonnes. ###### irreversible downward trend. 

In 2012, we expect the market balance to expand again on the back of the resumption of growth in global gold supply driven by rising mine output and a recovery in gold recycling in response to higher gold prices.  In part for the same reason, and partly because of the global economic slowdown, fabrication demand for gold is expected to shrink further this year, leaving a significant amount of metal for the investment sector to clear. 

As such, although we expect gold prices to resume their upward trend in the next six months, we believe that the net gain for this year as a whole is likely t

o be moderate.  Overall, we forecast that the gold price will average $1,680/oz in 2012, with a $1,710/oz average in the second half.

Even this forecast will require new investor buying, with the most likely trigger being the much-delayed introduction of a third round of quantitative easing in the USA.  As economic growth there remains lacklustre, we still expect QE3 to be instigated before year-end, with an accompanying rise in inflationary expectations.  Inflationary fears have always historically been supportive for gold. 

However, we are less certain about the strength of investor appetite in 2013 as potential buyers re-evaluate the risks that global financial markets face and as gold suffers from higher levels of investor fatigue.  The holders of shares in gold ETFs may be particularly sensitive to this change in mood, and could well switch from being net buyers to being modest net sellers in 2013.  Meanwhile, although falling further from its peak, gold’s fundamental surplus will still be sizeable in 2013, and we believe that this will at last begin to undermine quotations.  As in 2012, the year-on-year change may mask a much larger movement between January and December, although even the annual average could be lower next year, perhaps by 1% on a year-on-year basis. 

During the 2014-16 period, a sustained rise in interest rates and improvement in global economic conditions could prompt investors to intensify liquidation of their long positions in gold, putting more downward pressure on its price.  As gold’s descent accelerates, the cost pressures on fabrication demand should begin to ease, giving a boost to metal consumption. Meanwhile, lower prices may discourage gold recycling and therefore limit the expansion of the supply side.  As such, the size of the fundamental surplus is expected to decline steadily such that it totals only 1,087 tonnes in 2016. 

Overall, the average gold price over our forecast period is expected to equal $1,603/oz in nominal terms and $1,542/oz in real terms as quotations continue to slip year-on-year to at least 2016.

## 2.  Gold fabrication demand 

#### 2.1  Summary 

Our definition of fabrication demand includes demand for physical gold in the form of jewellery, coins and medallions, most of which is partly driven by the metal’s investment appeal.  True industrial uses are limited mainly to electronics, dental and a handful of minor applications. 

In 2012, we expect global fabrication demand to fall for the second consecutive year.  As in 2011, lacklustre demand for jewellery is likely to be the largest absolute driver of this decline. Record high gold prices in India as a result of rupee devaluation combined with restrictive measures that the Indian government has taken to curb domestic gold demand will almost certainly suppr

ess gold use in jewellery and medallion fabrication, as well as in some other applications in this key gold market. The vast size of the Indian gold market and high price sensitivity of local gold consumers means that, even if a small percentage of buyers decide to postpone their purchase of gold jewellery, it would result in a significant drop in actual physical demand. Admittedly, China’s growing love for luxury goods, including gold jewellery, will cushion the fall in demand from India, but we do not expect it to entirely offset it. Demand for gold emanating from any other industrial application, even on a global scale, is substantially lower compared with Indian demand for gold jewellery alone and therefore they cannot be relied upon to pick up the slack. In the current economic environment, there are still many households and investors around the world who feel financially insecure – to mitigate economic and financial risks they keep looking for safe-haven assets, of which gold coins is one of the obvious options. 

The pressure on fabrication demand may ease a little in 2013, when we expect gold prices to begin to move lower.  As such, we may see a bounce back in gold fabrication supported by the modest recovery in jewellery demand in India where the rupee might eventually strengthen against the US dollar.  In 2014 and 2015, we expect the recovery to accelerate driven by the continued fall in the gold price and improved economic conditions in the developed world which should further stimulate purchases of gold for use in jewellery and other industrial applications.  Still, the pace of recovery may slow down in the final year of our outlook as we expect the Chinese market to experience its first contraction in jewellery sales after many years of growth. 

Overall, we expect total fabrication demand for gold to get close to its pre-crisis 2007 level by 2016.  However, it may need another year or two before the recovery phase from the effects of the global financial crisis can be convincingly completed. 

#### 2.2  Jewellery fabri

cation 

###### **Introduction** 

Our statistics for jewellery consumption measure the gold content of new, carat jewellery and watches and are allocated between countries in line with final sales.  They exclude the gold contained in second-hand jewellery, gold-plated jewellery (which is included in industrial fabrication), coins and bars that are used as jewellery, and the part-exchange of existing for new pieces.  Global jewellery demand is driven by a combination of affordability and desirability. 

CRU International Limited confidential 

Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q2   Gold 

13 

Fabricators’ purchases of new and scrap gold will fluctuate around our totals for jewellery sales as manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers all adjust their stocks. 

In the developed world, gold jewellery is a luxury and discretionary adornment purchase rather than an investment.  Thus, it is positively related to disposable income and negatively related to price.  Before the latest economic downturn, these two factors more or less balanced out, and developed countries accounted for a fairly stable 22-25% of global jewellery consumption.  More recently, however, both absolute demand and its market share have collapsed such that only 9% of last year’s global purchases were located in Western Europe, North America and Japan. 

Developing countries, most notably India, China, the rest of Asia and the Middle East, now account for the vast bulk of global jewellery offtake.  In these countries, there can be a significant overlap between the adornment and savings and investment motives in jewellery purchases.  The jewellery bought in developing countries is typically of high purity (22 carat), non-branded and sold by weight at a relatively small margin over its contained metal cost. Consequently, changes in the gold price feed quickly through into that of finished jewellery. And consumers in these markets tend to be very price sensitive.  While there has been some move towards Western style products (most often imported and sold by piece) in many developing markets, this generally still comprises a small percentage of total sales. 

Factors influencing gold demand in developing countries include the gold price level and volatility (in US dollar and local currency terms), gold price expectations, cultural and social factors, disposable incomes, investor confidence, competition for discretionary spending from other luxury goods and services, design trends, tax and tariff changes on raw materials and finished products, the quality and price of competing finished jewellery products and any preference for alternative gold investment vehicles. 

However, it would be wrong to suppose that these factors interact identically in every country.  In India, for example, gold (and silver) jewellery is mainly viewed as a safe and portable vehicle for savings.  Money flows into the precious metal markets are therefore mainly a function of income, although the tonnages that these

money flows will purchase are inversely related to local prices, while the choice of which metal to buy will also be influenced by the ratios of different precious metal quotations.  At the other extreme, jewellery purchases in China and the Middle East have a very high investment motive, and may actually be encouraged by a clearly appreciating price. 

###### **Recent developments** 

Historically, jewellery has accounted for by far the greatest part of demand for gold. However, since the start of the 2000s, it has mostly been showing a downward trend in both absolute and proportional terms.  Between 2000 and 2011, global gold jewellery fabrication slid from 3,205 tonnes to 1,963 tonnes; as a share of the total fabrication, it declined from 85% to 71%, while the ratio of offtake to gold production slid from almost 1.0 to only 0.76. 

The fall was largely precipitated by shrinking demand in the developed world, where sales of gold jewellery were suppressed by an uninterrupted multiyear bull run in gold.  As already stated, most developed world consumers view gold jewellery as an adornment rather than an

investment.  For investment purposes, they tend to use other forms of gold, such as coins and bars or gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs).  Importantly, the latter are also backed by physical metal.  Investors in developed economies have therefore effectively been bidding gold away from local jewellery purchasers, this being the prime way in which the overall gold market has been brought to balance. 

Trends in jewellery consumption have been much more bullish outside the developed world, even in recent years.  Many of the key gold jewellery-buying markets have seen rapid GDP growth over the past decade, India and China being the most prominent examples.  This has led to a sharp increase in households’ disposable incomes and, as retail sectors in these countries have developed alongside, gold has been one of the many luxury consumer goods to benefit. For instance, per capita income in China rose from around the $3,000 level in 2000 to roughly $8,400 in 2011, and local demand for gold jewellery rose almost 2½-fold over the same period from 206 tonnes to 511 tonnes. 

In fact, the resumption of interest from Indian consumers and the ongoing growth of demand in China and Russia (markets of rapid income growth and market liberalisation, including liberalisation of the gold market) halted the global decline in jewellery fabrication around 2004. However, the downward trend reasserted itself in 2008, when more severe economic turmoil hit the world.  Jewellery demand plunged during the 2008-09 period as the global economic crisis prompted consumers to cut back their expenditure on luxury goods, including gold jewellery. In 2010, some positive signs appeared that gold jewellery demand had started to recuperate as the global economy began to recover from the financial c

risis of 2008-09.  Global demand bounced back by 11%, to 2,017 tonnes, despite gold prices jumping 26% in US dollar terms and rising in other currencies too.  In 2011, however, this nascent recovery was stalled by another round of double-digit increases in annual average gold prices; in US dollar terms the gold price soared by 28%.  At these price levels, consumers in some countries were not prepared to buy as much jewellery as they did in 2010 and, at best, demanded smaller, lighter pieces.  As a result, global demand decreased by 3% year-on-year to 1,963 tonnes.  Even so, the sector’s performance last year may still be considered relatively robust – in value terms, jewellery demand not only increased in 2011, but reached a new annual record of $99.2 billion, according to the World Gold Council (WGC). 

In terms of geographic distribution, India and China remained the cultural heartlands of gold, generating 55% of global jewellery demand last year.  Admittedly, this was not dissimilar to where these countries’ combined market share stood in 2010.  However, a closer look at each of these two key markets reveals that throughout 2011, particularly during its second half, jewellery demand in each country was driven by different sets of factors. 

Broadly speaking, demand from the two nations continued to strengthen in the first half of 2011.  Thankfully, good monsoon resulted in a bountiful harvest in India which, in combination with high grain prices, kept the national jewellery market buoyant.  The majority of India’s gold jewellery is purchased in rural areas, where farm income is heavily dependent on the harvest. A good monsoon is thus crucial to income.  Meanwhile, increasing prosperity among Chinese consumers, supported by very strong growth in the domestic economy, remained a driving force behind gold jewellery demand in that country.  Equally important was the fact that both India and China were facing increasing inflationary pressures due to rising food prices over that

period.  As such, some consumers flocked to gold jewellery as an inflation hedge whilst others continued to buy it as a luxury good. 

After holding up well in the first half of last year, a dichotomy began to appear between the two markets.  In response to the surge in gold prices above $1,500/oz last summer and very high price volatility, Indian demand began to weaken.  At the same time, the Reserve Bank of India, worried about spiralling inflation, continued to aggressively tighten its monetary policy.  This had severe consequences for the domestic jewellery market as the Indian rupee, following an initial rapid rise, plummeted in the second half of the year, on foreign capital outflows.  The rapid rise and fall in the rupee, and resulting domestic gold price swings, discouraged fresh buying.  We base this in part on the buying habits of Indian women, who account for the bulk of Ind

ian jewellery purchases.  High price volatility is a major deterrent to household gold purchases, as consumers withdraw from the market during periods of high price volatility for fear of overpaying.  Historically, high price volatility has noticeably affected Indian purchases. Thus, it probably came as little surprise that even the Diwali festival, which is considered by Indians as a key gold buying occasion and traditionally takes place sometime between the middle of October and the middle of December of each year, failed to lift the country’s gold jewellery demand.  Despite falling in US dollar terms during the festivities, gold reached record levels in rupee terms, depressing price-sensitive consumer demand and encouraging recycling instead.  As a result of these developments, annual jewellery demand in India, the world’s largest market for gold, dropped to 567 tonnes, or 14% below 2010 levels. 

Meanwhile, in China, the second largest gold market, annual demand continued to grow steadily throughout last year.  Compared with India, Chinese jewellery purchases have a significantly stronger investment component, and it is difficult to delineate between jewellery demand for adornment purposes and purchases in which investment is the primary focus.  As such, China’s rising prosperity along with escalating consumer inflation, negative real rates on savings and expectations of further gold price appreciation were stimulating gold jewellery demand in this country throughout the whole year.  Besides that, in the final months of 2011, the renminbi, in contrast to the rupee, strengthened against the US dollar instead of weakening, providing support to domestic demand.  All in all, the annual gold jewellery consumption in China went up by 13% in 2011, to 511 tonnes.  It is worth noting that at this level, last year’s consumption in China represented 90% of India’s annual demand.  This figure exceeded the 50% mark only four years ago, in 2007.  This rapid growth in such a short period reflects how voracious the appetite for gold jewellery in China is. 

As for other regional markets, 2011 demand in the Middle East was constrained by high prices and regional political turmoil, which adversely affected demand for luxury goods, including gold jewellery.  As a result, demand declined by 19% to 166 tonnes.  In North America, gold jewellery continued its long-term downward path with last year’s demand down 10% to 115 tonnes.  High and very volatile prices for the precious metal, a fragile labour market, depressed real estate prices and volatile stock market all contributed to hesitant consumer demand and fragile consumer confidence.  Perhaps unsurprisingly, the Western European market, bogged down in sovereign debt crisis, suffered the most as reflected by the highest percent decline with purchases for last year collapsing by 33% to 65 tonnes.  Sluggish economic growth and high unemployment resulted in limited increases in real income and

undermined consumer confidence which, in turn, weighed on gold jewellery consumption in this region. 

On balance, strong interest in gold jewellery emanating from China and some other regional markets such as Hong Kong, Russia and Turkey more than offset demand weakness in such areas as North America and Western Europe.  But the gains were not large enough to compensate for lacklustre Indian demand, leading to a net contraction of the global gold jewellery market in 2011. 

The dichotomy established last year between the Indian and Chinese markets has also continued into 2012.  While the gold price has been weak in US dollar terms since the start of March 2012, fresh weakness in the rupee over the same period means that the gold price has continued to rise in rupee terms, resulting in lower jewellery sales.  More worryingly, since the beginning of this year, the Indian government has been demonstrating increasing unease with its current balance of payments falling deeper into deficit.  Having identified Indian’s affinity for gold as a major force driving the country into debt (India does not produce much gold itself and therefore imports are the only source of new supply to the domestic market), officials have explicitly started to target gold demand: on two occasions this year the government has increased import tariffs and imposed an excise duty on gold jewellery.  The announcement of these measures sparked a country-wide strike among jewellers which lasted for three weeks in March-April and came to the end only when the Finance Minister promised to abolish the proposed excise duty.  Additionally, the Indian government is looking to restrict gold loans where money is leant against gold, including its jewellery form, as collateral.  It is concerned about the involvement of non-bank finance companies and the impact on the stability of the financial system. ###### **Forecast production** 

Until recently, the long lag time between investment and output has been masking gold miners’ response to higher prices.  But, having hit record high levels of output in the last two years, the global gold mining industry appears to be reversing a decade-long trend of weak and unstable production. 

Indeed, thanks to higher gold prices, gold miners are extremely motivated to increase gold output even despite a range of obstacles they continue to face.  These include declining ore grades, rising costs, increased government and environmental regulations, and reserves that are increasingly difficult to access, not to mention a shortage of skilled technical specialists. Although addressing these challenges is not a quick and easy task, at current price levels, which are well above the cost of production, gold miners can still overcome escalating costs relatively

comfortably and therefore risk re-starting operations at some mines which had to be mothballed earlier for economic reasons or even bring into production projects that would have been rejected as too expensive just a couple of years ago. Also, more gold production is scheduled to come on stream during the next few years as investments made earlier in the mining cycle translate into greater output. Importantly, the miners are not stopping laying the groundwork for future expansion and keep investing in exploration and mine development as they try to make up for lost time. According to the _Metals Economics Group_ , the estimated total spending on nonferrous metals exploration in 2011 reached a record $18.2 billion, up around 50% from $12.1 billion in 2010. Noteworthy, gold projects received the largest portion of investment, accounting for about half of the global exploration budget for the second year in a row. The sheer scale of exploration dollars being injected into the gold mining industry makes us think that the output trajectory for at least the next five years is likely to be higher. Underpinning this, exploration spending dedicated to early-stage work has been at historically low levels for the last three years, while late-stage and mine-site budgets have been receiving a higher proportion of spending. This reflects the desire of gold miners to push nearterm production forward, even if this comes at the expense of future output. Mining companies sometimes sell forward a portion of their future production to a financial institution in order to gain finance for a new mining project or to guarantee future sales receipts. A producer may choose

to undertake hedging activity to provide protection against an expected decline in the gold price.  Conversely, if the gold price is expected to rise, it may choose to unwind its existing hedge book to gain exposure to the benefits of that increase.  A mining company’s gold hedge book comprises the total set of positions it holds as gold forward sales, options and other derivative instruments.  Changes to these positions have an impact on the spot physical gold market, typically through gold leasing arrangements. 

There are three main parties involved in a basic gold hedge contract: the producer; a bullion bank, which acts as the producer’s dealer; and a central bank.  To place a hedge, the producer advises its dealer that it wishes to forward sell, for example, one tonne of metal.  The dealer then borrows this amount from a central bank (paying a leasing fee), which it immediately sells into the spot market, agreeing to return the one tonne by a certain date.  The proceeds from this sale are then placed in a high-yielding cash account (subtracting the dealer’s fee and the leasing fee on the borrowed gold), usually generating a premium for the producer.  The producer is obliged to return the one tonne of gold to the bullion bank by the pre-agreed date.  At the time of implementation, the bullion bank’s borrowing of the gold and selling it into the spot market increases the supply of gold to the market.  However, when the gold is returned, usually by delivering mine production from the producer’s account, supply reaching the market is correspondingly constrained.  Hedging activity therefore represents an acceleration of supply to the market, but the overall balance of supply and demand is maintained over the lifetime of the transaction. 

The 1990s were largely characterised by unrelenting downward pressure on the gold price, which led to steadily increasing levels of hedging undertaken by producers who were seeking revenue protection from further declines.  In 1995, hedging had a particularly noticeable impact, reaching 475 tonnes and thereby accounting for about 13% of total supply. 

Producers’ reversal in hedging policies dates back to the beginning of the current bull cycle in 2000-01.  When the gold price had made an abrupt change of direction and started to climb, many hedged producers were caught off-guard and were unable to take advantage of soaring spot prices.  On the back of this, 2000 was the first year since the late 1970s when the global producer hedge book did not expand.  There has since been a protracted period of de-hedging, in which producers have both delivered into and prematurely closed out their hedge contracts. This has been accomplished either by bullion purchases from the market, delivered to the bullion bank, or through delivering their own production into contracts before they mature.  Dehedging hit a record of 444 tonnes in 2007, removing 12% from total gold supply.  Expectations for higher gold prices and mining co

mpany investors’ associated anti-hedging sentiment were the chief reasons for this. 

Prior to 2000, producer hedging was thus a significant supply component in the gold market whereas, post-2000, hedging activity acted to tighten the fundamental balance.  Having said this, the pace of producer buybacks has slowed markedly in recent years, as a greatly diminished global hedge book has left producers with little in the way of hedge positions to close out. As producer de-hedging slowly fades, an important constraint on available supply has gradually been removed from the market.

#### 4.1  Recent price developments 

In 2011, gold posted its tenth consecutive year of annual price gains – at $1,571/oz its average for the year was 28% higher than in 2010.  This was gold’s second strongest annual performance in relative terms during this bull run, beaten only by the rise of 36% registered in 2006, but that was from a much lower base. Not every investor managed to profit from t

Having started the year at $1,388/oz, gold initially weakened as economic sentiment temporarily improved, with the gold price hitting its low for the year of $1,319/oz in late January.  From there, it started to move higher as the global political and economical situation continued to worsen.  The upward move accelerated in July as concerns grew about the outcome of negotiations between the US Administration and Congress over the country’s debt ceiling ahead of its deadline on 2 August.  Although both parties eventually came to an agreement and the ceiling was raised, market confidence in the ability of the US officials to perform their duties efficiently was severely dented; on 5 August, the US credit rating was downgraded to less than AAA for the first time in its history.  As the US dollar, one of gold’s major competitors as a safe haven, was taking a hit, the price of the precious metal exploded to new nominal highs. 

Meanwhile, on the other side of the Atlantic, Europe was trying to solve its own financial conundrum as the mounting sovereign debt problems raised worries about a double dip in the region’s economic activity.  As the euro weakened, the Swiss National Bank intervened in early September and set a ceiling for the Swiss franc at 1.20 to the euro in an attempt to prevent its economy from being dragged into recession by the strength of its currency.  With another safehaven asset effectively off their radar, investors flocked into gold anticipating imminent financial Armageddon.  As a result, the metal reached an intraday high of $1,920/oz on 6 September. 

Shortly after the IMF expressed its concerns about the future prospects for the global economy in its Global Financial Stability report in mid-September, worries over the inevitability of another, perhaps even larger, global recession unnerved investors in virtually all financial markets.  And this led to a period of risk aversion along with widespread asset liquidation as investors raced for cash.  The massive size of this liquidation sparked a wave of margin calls leaving many investors and funds in desperate need for cash to meet their financial obligations. In order to raise this money, many decided to dump gold which is a great source of liquidity during the tight times.
